extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers studying Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Aristotle's evaluative criteria for voluntary action, moral choice (prohairesis), deliberation, responsibility, formation of virtue, and the virtue of Courage as a mean between excess and deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs Involuntary Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes actions that are voluntary from those strictly involuntary; strictly involuntary actions are attended with pain, while actions done to gratify lust are pleasant and not properly involuntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions done from anger or lust are not to be classed as strictly involuntary; involuntariness is associated with external compulsion or ignorance (not self-caused). Examples and consequences: lawgivers and communities treat voluntary acts as subject to praise or blame, while clearly involuntary acts are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice (Prohairesis) is Voluntary but Distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is plainly voluntary but not co-extensive with voluntary action; children and animals may act voluntarily without moral choice, and sudden actions may be voluntary without being moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Choice involves a prior deliberative process and selection among alternatives; it is a 'grasping after something in our own power consequent upon Deliberation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice is not Lust, Anger, Wish, or Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is distinct from lust and anger (which animals share), from wish (which may have impossible ends), and from opinion (which is true/false rather than good/bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: those lacking self-control act from lust not moral choice; wish concerns ends (possibly impossible), moral choice concerns means; opinion does not by itself form character as choosing does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice Concerns Means, Not Ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation and Moral Choice are about the means to ends rather than about ends themselves; one deliberates how to achieve a chosen end, not whether to have the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physicians do not deliberate whether to cure (end) but how to cure (means); the object of Moral Choice is something in our own power (means).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation's Proper Objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation concerns practical matters that can be effected through one's own instrumentality and are neither eternal, necessary, purely variable, nor fortuitous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deliberate about eternal truths, fixed natural events (solstices), purely variable weather, or chance events; deliberate about matters under general laws but with some indefiniteness and where our actions can influence the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation Excludes Exact Sciences/Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation is not employed for exact, fully determined arts or minute sensible details (e.g., how a written character must be formed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation applies to arts more than to exact sciences because arts leave more room for judgment about means; it also stops when the origination is brought up to the governing principle in the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation as Search and Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation is a searching, analytical process that examines possible instruments and methods; if impossibility is discovered, the attempt is abandoned; if possibility appears, action is attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agent considers what may be done through own instrumentality and analyses 'through what' and 'how' until reaching feasible means; deliberation is preparatory to choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Wish vs Objects of Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Wish has the End as its object (what one desires, possibly impossible), while Moral Choice has the means to the End as its object and concerns things one can himself procure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wish may aim at impossibilities (immortality) or at ends one cannot achieve; Moral Choice is restricted to things believed to be achievable by the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion vs Moral Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion is exercised over a wide range of objects (including impossible/eternal things) and is divided true/false; Moral Choice is about good/bad and forms character, not merely belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion may precede or accompany choice but is not identical with Moral Choice; one may hold correct opinion yet choose badly because of viciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues as Mean States and Habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues are mean states between excess and deficiency, are habits formed by repeated acts, and are developed by practice (acts of working).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue's number and relation to objects will be determined by examining each virtue; the habit determines the end and governs particular acts (habit formed by many small actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and Vice are in Our Power (Responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because actions and the formation of habits are within our power, both virtue and vice are voluntary and thus subject to praise or blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if one no longer can change a formed habit, the origination of that habit was once in one's power; legal and moral systems punish self-caused ignorance (e.g., drunkenness) as blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for Self-Caused Ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance that is self-caused (e.g., through drunkenness or neglect of duties that one could have known) is blameworthy and makes actions voluntary for which one is responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heavier penalties for the drunken; those who neglect to learn the law they are bound to know are chastised; ignorance that stems from carelessness is a sign of stupidity and culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice Requires Some Knowledge and Prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is attended with reasoning and intellectual process; it presupposes a sensible man's deliberation about achievable means, not the ignorant or mad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etymology: the Greek name suggests 'chosen in preference to somewhat else'; moral choice involves forming character by choosing goods and avoiding bads in light of reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Courage as a Mean Relative to Fear and Confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is a mean state with respect to fear and boldness (confidence) concerning honourable dangers; the Brave man faces right objects of fear from the right motive, in the right manner and at the right time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary object-matter: things fearful that are noble/honourable (e.g., death in war). The Brave man resists fear as reason directs and for the sake of honour; excess = rashness (too much confidence), deficiency = cowardice (too much fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Objects, Motive, Manner, and Time for Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is Brave if he withstands or acts with respect to proper objects, from a proper motive (honour), in the proper manner, and at the proper times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors include fearing when one ought not to, fearing in an improper way, at wrong times, or fearing wrong objects; right reason should direct courageous action toward honourable ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of Types/Imitations of Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Various dispositions bearing the name 'Courage' are distinguished: civic/citizen courage (motivated by honour/disgrace), courage from compulsion (lower because fear of pain drives it), courage from experience/skill, animal spirit, and those acting from anger or lust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether brave actions stem from a sense of honour and moral choice (true courage) versus compulsion, mere training/skill, instinctive animal spirit, or passion; examples: Homeric heroes for civic courage; regular troops vs militia; wild beasts and profligates lack true moral choice.
